extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians, comedy fans, and readers interested in live comedy and viral video culture
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and judgments for how stand-up comedians perform crowd work (interacting with audience members), especially as those moments are shaped for viral social-media clips. Focuses on authenticity, target selection, comedic skill, and platform incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / no manufactured conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid "manufactured moments of conflict" with audience members meant solely to generate viral content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece repeatedly criticizes comics who "manufactur[e] moments of conflict" because social platforms reward "heckler destruction" clips. Guidance: prefer genuine interactions over staged baiting; recognize that forcing conflict for algorithmic gain is a negative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to elicit a genuine reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful crowd work should provoke a real response from the audience rather than begging someone to react (the subject "failed to provoke the woman into reacting").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an interaction produces no real emotional payoff (silence/unamused faces), it reads as a failure. Effective crowd work produces observable engagement rather than one-sided attempts for attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skillful, spontaneous parrying (clap-backs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good crowd work is "a comedian reacting to an unruly audience member and parrying their outbursts with perfect clap-backs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians should be able to improvise clever retorts that restore control and land as jokes; simply shouting insults or repeating tropes is not the same as a skilled comeback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real jokes, not attention-seeking monologues
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd work should consist of comedic material, not "not quite jokes. More like cries for attention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid turning interactions into self-serving attempts to solicit outrage or views; the exchange should have humor and craft rather than desperation for a reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality — avoid recycled trolling lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't mentally run down the same "laundry list" of stock 'triggering' accusations and insults used by unfunny trolls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on predictable, derivative attacks (the same lines other performers/trolls use) signals weak crowd work. Strive for original observations and responses rather than rote baiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate target selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose whom you engage with carefully — singling out a quiet, unamused person can backfire (he "singled out a quiet, unamused woman" who remained unbothered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeting an audience member who is unlikely to react or who is inappropriate to provoke will make the performer look bad; pick moments/people who can plausibly play along or where engagement is likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fabricating audience content
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't invent claims about what the crowd said ("You know your crowd work is terrible when you have to make up the things said by the crowd").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present interactions honestly. Making up crowd lines or attributing words to audience members undermines credibility and signals poor material or insecure performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of platform incentives (don't perform just for algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that "the algorithms of every content platform reward crowd work clips" and that this can drive comics to manufacture conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While platforms favor certain formats, creators should avoid altering craft solely to chase engagement. Prioritize comedic quality over creating spectacle purely for virality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offstage conduct and reputation influence reception
rubrics_metrics.description: A performer's prior behavior (e.g., controversial or harmful actions) affects how crowd work is received — referenced by Bankas' past of "getting booted... for cheering on the fatal shooting".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience and online communities contextualize performances with a comedian's reputation; past misconduct can magnify backlash and shape interpretation of onstage interactions.
